qualification: Namibia Senior Secondary Certificate Advanced Subsidiary level (NSSCAS) Biology 8223 (syllabus vNIED 2020, examined 2021-2025)

items.prompt: A learner is given the aim: to find the effect of the temperature of a water bath on the time that milk takes to clot after rennet is added (our own situation). Describe, in order, the steps used to decide which variable is independent and which is dependent, and state the answer.
items.canonical_answer: First find the two quantities named in the aim, the temperature of the water bath and the time to clot. Then ask which one the learner sets: the temperature is chosen by the learner, so it is the independent variable. Then ask which one is recorded: the time to clot is read from a stopwatch, so it is the dependent variable. The result is temperature in °C as the independent variable and time in s as the dependent variable.
marking_guidance: 3 marks: the two quantities picked out of the aim, temperature and time to clot (1); the test applied in order, the variable that is set is the independent one, so temperature (1); the variable that is recorded is the dependent one, so time to clot, as the final result (1).
An answer that gives the two variables with no step or test earns the last two marks only if the order of the decision is clear. Swapping the two variables earns no mark for the result.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.1 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and readings are our own and unverified.
objective_titles: Identify the independent and dependent variables in an investigation.

items.prompt: State the reason for changing just one independent variable at a time in an investigation.
items.canonical_answer: If one independent variable is changed at a time, any change in the dependent variable can be put down to it. If two were changed together, the change could come from either one.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the reason, that the change in the dependent variable can then be attributed to the one variable that was changed, because otherwise either could have caused it.
A statement that this makes the investigation fair, with no reason, earns no mark.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.1 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and readings are our own and unverified.
objective_titles: Identify the independent and dependent variables in an investigation.

items.prompt: A learner heats tubes of an enzyme and its substrate at 20, 40 and 60 °C and uses a buffer of pH 5 in the first tube, pH 7 in the second and pH 9 in the third (our own situation). The learner records the time for the substrate to be broken down in each tube. Describe the limitation of this design.
items.canonical_answer: Both the temperature and the pH change between the tubes, so there are two independent variables. A difference in the times could be an effect of the temperature or of the pH, and the results cannot show which. The design needs the pH to be the same in all three tubes when the temperature is changed.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the limitation named, two variables are changed together (1); the effect on the conclusion, the difference in time cannot be attributed to the temperature or to the pH, because either could have caused it (1).
An answer that says the test is not fair, with no effect on the conclusion, earns the first mark at most. The error is a design error, not a measuring error.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.1 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and readings are our own and unverified.
objective_titles: Identify the independent and dependent variables in an investigation.

items.prompt: In an investigation of how the distance of a lamp from a pondweed plant affects the number of bubbles released in 5 minutes, a learner says that the dependent variable is the volume of water in each beaker, because it is the thing that is kept the same (our own situation). Explain the error in this statement.
items.canonical_answer: The error is a confusion of the dependent variable with a standardised variable. In fact the volume of water is kept the same in every beaker, so it is a standardised variable and it is not recorded as a result. The test is to ask which variable is set and which is recorded: the distance of the lamp is set, so it is independent, and the number of bubbles in 5 minutes is recorded, so it is the dependent variable.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the error named, a variable that is kept the same is confused with the dependent variable, which is the one that is measured (1); the correct idea or the test that tells them apart, the lamp distance is set and the bubbles are recorded, so bubbles are dependent (1).

The card is a discrimination between two different kinds of variable and not a repeat of the definition. Instead of naming the bubbles, an answer that names the lamp distance as dependent has repeated the first confusion.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.1 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and readings are our own and unverified.
objective_titles: Identify the independent and dependent variables in an investigation.

items.prompt: A learner has a stock solution of sucrose of 1.0 mol dm⁻³ and needs five solutions of 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 and 1.0 mol dm⁻³, each of 10 cm³ in total (our own situation). Describe, in order, how the five solutions are made by proportional dilution.
items.canonical_answer: First measure 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 cm³ of the stock solution into five tubes with a syringe. Then add 8, 6, 4, 2 and 0 cm³ of water with a clean syringe so that each tube holds 10 cm³ in total, and mix. The concentration of each follows from volume of stock ÷ total volume × concentration of stock, for example 4 ÷ 10 × 1.0 = 0.4 mol dm⁻³, so the five concentrations are 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 and 1.0 mol dm⁻³.
marking_guidance: 3 marks: the volumes of stock, 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 cm³, measured with a syringe or pipette, as the first step (1); the volume of water that brings each tube to 10 cm³ in total, as the next step (1); the concentration checked from the equation, stock volume ÷ total volume × stock concentration, so the result matches the five values (1).
Adding the same volume of water to each tube does not give the five values and earns no mark for the water step.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.1 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and readings are our own and unverified.
objective_titles: Decide how to change the independent variable over a suitable range.

items.prompt: State why a buffer solution is used to set the pH of each mixture in an investigation of the effect of pH on the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction.
items.canonical_answer: A buffer holds the pH close to its set value, so the pH stays the same while the reaction goes on. Adding acid or alkali to the mixture would let the pH drift as the reaction proceeds.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the reason, a buffer resists a change in pH, so the pH stays at the set value throughout the reaction, because it would drift if acid or alkali were added.
A statement that a buffer makes the solution acidic or alkaline earns no mark.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.1 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and readings are our own and unverified.
objective_titles: Decide how to change the independent variable over a suitable range.

items.prompt: A learner investigates how the temperature of water affects the time that an effervescent tablet takes to dissolve and uses water at 20, 22, 24, 26 and 28 °C (our own situation). Describe a limitation of this range of temperatures.
items.canonical_answer: The range covers only 8 °C, so the change in the time to dissolve may be small compared with the random differences between repeat readings, and the pattern may not be visible. Nothing is learnt about what happens at higher or lower temperatures, so the effect of temperature is not fully described. A wider range, such as 10 to 60 °C, would show the pattern.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the limitation named, the range is narrow (8 °C) (1); the effect, the change in time may be lost among the random differences, or the pattern outside the range is not known, because no values were taken there (1).
An answer that says more values are needed is about the number of values and not the range, and earns no mark.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.1 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and readings are our own and unverified.
objective_titles: Decide how to change the independent variable over a suitable range.

items.prompt: A learner will record the mass lost by a leafy shoot in 30 minutes with a fan placed at different distances from the shoot, between 0.25 m and 1.25 m (our own situation). Describe, in order, how the number and spacing of the distances are chosen.
items.canonical_answer: First choose the range, 0.25 m to 1.25 m. Then space the distances equally at 0.25 m, which gives 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00 and 1.25 m. The span is 1.25 − 0.25 = 1.00 m, and 1.00 ÷ 0.25 = 4 intervals, so 4 + 1 = 5 values, which is the minimum number needed to see the pattern. Finally, if the mass lost changes most between two distances, add one or more values between them, so that the change is found more closely.
marking_guidance: 3 marks: the range stated and the values spaced at equal intervals (1); the count of 5 values, the minimum, shown from the span and the interval (1); extra values added around the distances where the result changes most, as the final step (1).
A plan with fewer than 5 values earns no mark for the count, because a straight line cannot then be told from a curve.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.1 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and readings are our own and unverified.
objective_titles: Decide how many values to measure at, and where to take more.

items.prompt: State why at least five values of the independent variable are used in an investigation, rather than two or three.
items.canonical_answer: Five or more points show whether the dependent variable follows a straight line, a curve or a peak, and a point that does not fit stands out. With two or three points these patterns cannot be told apart.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the reason, enough points are needed to see the shape of the pattern, because two or three points fit more than one pattern.
An answer that says more values make the result more accurate, with no reference to the pattern, earns no mark.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.1 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and readings are our own and unverified.
objective_titles: Decide how many values to measure at, and where to take more.

items.prompt: A learner measures the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction at 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 °C and finds the fastest rate at 40 °C, with a lower rate at both 30 and 50 °C (our own situation). Describe a limitation of stopping at these five values.
items.canonical_answer: The temperature of the fastest rate lies somewhere between 30 and 50 °C, but a gap of 10 °C on each side was left with no readings, so the peak is not located more closely than that. Extra values at 35 and 45 °C would narrow it to within 5 °C, so the effect is a more exact estimate of the best temperature.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the limitation named, no values were taken between 30 and 40 °C or between 40 and 50 °C, so the position of the peak is uncertain by up to 10 °C (1); the effect or the improvement, extra values around 40 °C such as 35 and 45 °C, which locate the peak more closely (1).
An answer that adds values at 0 °C or 100 °C does not address the limitation and earns no mark.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.1 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and readings are our own and unverified.
objective_titles: Decide how many values to measure at, and where to take more.

items.prompt: Describe, in order, how a sample of milk is tested for protein with biuret reagent, and state the result that shows protein is present.
items.canonical_answer: First place about 2 cm³ of the milk in a clean test tube. Then add biuret reagent and mix gently. Then watch the colour. If protein is present the mixture turns from blue to purple or lilac, which is the result of a positive test; if protein is absent it stays blue.
marking_guidance: 3 marks: the sample placed in a tube and the reagent added and mixed, as the first steps (1); the mixture observed, with no heating needed, as the next step (1); the result, blue to purple or lilac when protein is present and stays blue when absent (1).
Heating the tube is a step of the Benedict's test and earns no mark here. A colour named without the starting colour earns the result mark only if it is purple or lilac.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.1 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and readings are our own and unverified.
objective_titles: Decide how to identify a biological molecule and estimate its quantity by standardising a test.

items.prompt: A learner estimates the sugar in a sample by comparing its Benedict's colour with the colours of standard solutions of known concentration. State the reason for using the same volume of reagent and the same heating time for the sample and for every standard.
items.canonical_answer: The colour should depend only on the amount of sugar. A different volume of reagent or a different time in the hot water bath would change the colour, so the sample and the standards could not be compared fairly.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the reason, the colour must be due to the concentration of sugar and not to the method, because a different volume or time changes the colour, so the comparison would not be fair.
A statement that the test must be a fair test, with no link to the colour, earns no mark.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.1 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and readings are our own and unverified.
objective_titles: Decide how to identify a biological molecule and estimate its quantity by standardising a test.

items.prompt: A learner estimates the vitamin C in orange juice by adding juice from a pipette, a few drops at a time, to 1.0 cm³ of blue DCPIP solution until the blue colour has gone, and records the volume of juice used (our own situation). Describe a limitation of this method.
items.canonical_answer: The end-point is judged by eye, and the exact drop at which the last of the blue colour goes is hard to see. The volume recorded may be too large by a few drops, so the estimate of the concentration of vitamin C is less accurate. A colorimeter or a white tile behind the tube would help.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the limitation named, the end-point is a colour change judged by eye, which is difficult to see exactly (1); the effect, the volume of juice is uncertain by a few drops, so the concentration estimated from it is inaccurate (1).
An answer about the pipette being dirty is a different error and earns no mark unless it is linked to the end-point.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.1 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and readings are our own and unverified.
objective_titles: Decide how to identify a biological molecule and estimate its quantity by standardising a test.

items.prompt: In an investigation, 2.0 cm³ of a standard solution of ascorbic acid of 1.0 mg cm⁻³ removed the blue colour of a fixed volume of DCPIP solution. A juice removed the same colour from the same volume and concentration of DCPIP when 4.0 cm³ of the juice was added (our own invented values). Explain, with working, why the juice has a lower concentration of vitamin C than the standard, and calculate its concentration.
items.canonical_answer: The amount of vitamin C that removes the colour is the same each time. From the standard, 1.0 × 2.0 = 2.0 mg. In this case the juice needed 4.0 cm³ to supply that same 2.0 mg, so its concentration is 2.0 ÷ 4.0 = 0.5 mg cm⁻³. This is half the concentration of the standard, because twice the volume was needed to supply the same amount.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the reason from the data, the same amount of vitamin C, 2.0 mg, is needed each time, so a larger volume of juice means a lower concentration (1); the working and final answer with the unit, 2.0 ÷ 4.0 = 0.5 mg cm⁻³ (1).
An answer of 0.5 with no unit loses the second mark. A calculation that divides 4.0 by 2.0 gives 2.0 and has the relationship the wrong way round.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.1 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and readings are our own and unverified.
objective_titles: Decide how to identify a biological molecule and estimate its quantity by standardising a test.

items.prompt: A learner investigates the effect of an amylase solution on a starch solution in a water bath at 35 °C (our own situation). Describe, in order, how the control is set up and what result it should give.
items.canonical_answer: First place the same volume of starch solution in a tube, and replace the amylase solution with the same volume of water. Then put the tube in the same water bath at 35 °C for the same time and test it with iodine in the same way. The result is that the starch is still present, shown by the blue-black colour, so the loss of starch in the main tube is due to the amylase.
marking_guidance: 3 marks: the amylase solution replaced by the same volume of water, the first step (1); the control treated in the same way as the main tube, the same bath, time and test, as the next step (1); the result, starch is still present, so the change in the main tube is due to the amylase (1).
A control tube kept at room temperature differs in a second way and earns no mark for the second point.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.1 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and readings are our own and unverified.
objective_titles: Describe an appropriate control and the variables to standardise.

items.prompt: State why the enzyme solution is boiled before it is used in a control tube.
items.canonical_answer: Boiling destroys the shape of the active site permanently, so the enzyme cannot work. The control then has the same volume of solution and the other conditions as the main tube, but without the effect of the active enzyme.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the reason, the boiled enzyme no longer works because its active site is permanently changed, so the effect of the enzyme is removed, because everything else is the same.
A statement that boiling kills the enzyme earns the mark only if it says that the enzyme stops working. Enzymes are not living, so killing is not the correct term.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.1 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and readings are our own and unverified.
objective_titles: Describe an appropriate control and the variables to standardise.

items.prompt: A learner uses a boiled enzyme solution as the control for a test tube of active enzyme held in a water bath at 35 °C for 10 minutes, but leaves the control tube on the bench at room temperature (our own situation). Describe the limitation of this control.
items.canonical_answer: The control differs from the main tube in the temperature as well as in the enzyme, because it was not in the bath. If the substrate in the control behaves differently, the cause could be the lower temperature and not the missing enzyme, so the result cannot be compared. The control must be held in the same bath for the same time.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the limitation named, the control was treated differently, in the temperature (1); the effect, the difference from the main tube could be due to the temperature as well as the enzyme, so it cannot be attributed to the enzyme alone (1).
An answer that says the enzyme has to be boiled for longer does not address the limitation and earns no mark.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.1 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and readings are our own and unverified.
objective_titles: Describe an appropriate control and the variables to standardise.

items.prompt: A learner moves a fan to different distances from a leafy bean shoot and records the mass lost in 20 minutes (our own situation). Describe, in order, how the learner standardises the size of the shoot, the light and the temperature near the shoot.
items.canonical_answer: First choose shoots from one plant with the same number of leaves and of similar height, so that the size is the same. Then place every shoot on the same bench under the same lamp at a fixed distance, so that the light is the same. Then read a thermometer near the shoot at the start and the end of each run, and keep the room at one temperature, so that the temperature is the same. The result is that only the distance of the fan differs.
marking_guidance: 3 marks: each variable named with a method that fits it, size by shoots of one batch with the same number of leaves (1); light by a lamp at a fixed distance and the same place (1); temperature checked with a thermometer, as the final step (1).
An answer that says keep each variable the same, with no method, earns no mark. The order of the steps is credited where the sequence is clear, so the result is that only the fan distance differs.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.1 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and readings are our own and unverified.
objective_titles: Decide which variables to standardise and how.

items.prompt: State why the temperature of the tubes is kept the same in an investigation of the effect of enzyme concentration on the rate of a reaction.
items.canonical_answer: Temperature affects the rate of the reaction, so if it changed between the tubes the change in the rate could not be put down to the enzyme concentration alone.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the reason, temperature affects the rate, because a change in temperature would be a second cause, so the change in rate could not be attributed to the enzyme concentration.
A statement that it makes the test fair earns no mark without the reason.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.1 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and readings are our own and unverified.
objective_titles: Decide which variables to standardise and how.

items.prompt: A learner tries to keep the temperature of tubes at 35 °C with a beaker of warm water on the bench and does not add hot water again. After 10 minutes the water has cooled to 28 °C (our own situation). Describe the limitation of this method of standardising temperature.
items.canonical_answer: The temperature is not the same throughout the investigation: it falls from 35 to 28 °C, a fall of 7 °C. The rate of the reaction changes as the temperature falls, so the readings taken later are lower than they would be at 35 °C, which is an error that is not due to the independent variable. A thermostatic water bath, or checking the thermometer and adding warm water, keeps it constant.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the limitation named, the temperature changes during the work, from 35 to 28 °C, so it is not standardised (1); the effect on the result, the rate of the reaction changes with the temperature, so later readings are in error, because the change is not due to the independent variable (1).
An answer that says the beaker is too small does not state the effect and earns no mark.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.1 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and readings are our own and unverified.
objective_titles: Decide which variables to standardise and how.

items.prompt: Yeast in sugar solution releases carbon dioxide, which is collected in a gas syringe marked every 1 cm³ for 5 minutes (our own situation). Describe, in order, how the volume of gas is measured so that the reading is accurate.
items.canonical_answer: First check that the plunger of the syringe is at 0 cm³ and that the joints do not leak. Then add the yeast, start the stopwatch as the bung goes in, and leave the apparatus without moving it. At the end of 5 minutes read the volume at the end of the plunger with the eye level with the mark, and record it in cm³ to the nearest division, 1 cm³. The result is a reading that is not altered by gas escaping or by a misread mark.
marking_guidance: 3 marks: the set-up checked, the plunger at zero and no leaks, as the first step (1); the stopwatch started when the bung is in and the volume read at 5 minutes (1); the reading taken with the eye level with the mark and recorded to the nearest division with its unit, so the result is accurate (1).
A reading taken from above or below the mark is a parallax error and earns no mark for the last point.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.1 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and readings are our own and unverified.
objective_titles: Decide and describe how to measure the dependent variable accurately and precisely.

items.prompt: State why a syringe marked every 0.1 cm³ is a better choice than a measuring cylinder marked every 5 cm³ for measuring a volume of about 2 cm³.
items.canonical_answer: The syringe has small scale divisions, so it can be read to the nearest 0.1 cm³ and can separate volumes such as 2.0 and 2.3 cm³. A cylinder marked every 5 cm³ cannot separate them, because the divisions are larger than the volume.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the reason, the smaller divisions of the syringe let a volume of about 2 cm³ be read to 0.1 cm³, so the measurement is more precise, because the divisions of the cylinder are larger than the volume.
An answer that says the syringe is more accurate earns the mark only if it refers to the division size.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.1 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and readings are our own and unverified.
objective_titles: Decide and describe how to measure the dependent variable accurately and precisely.

items.prompt: A learner times the point at which a blue colour disappears from a tube by watching the tube and stopping a stopwatch that reads to 0.01 s (our own situation). Describe a limitation of timings recorded to 0.01 s.
items.canonical_answer: The learner judges when the colour has gone and then presses the button, and the judgement and the delay in pressing are typically a few tenths of a second. So the uncertainty of the timing is much larger than 0.01 s, and recording to 0.01 s claims more precision than the method has. The effect is that the readings cannot be trusted beyond the nearest 0.1 s.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the limitation named, the end-point is judged by eye and the stopwatch is stopped by hand, so there is an error of a few tenths of a second (1); the effect, recording to 0.01 s claims a precision the method does not have, so the readings are less precise than they appear (1).
An answer that says the stopwatch is not accurate earns no mark, because the error comes from the person and not from the stopwatch.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.1 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and readings are our own and unverified.
objective_titles: Decide and describe how to measure the dependent variable accurately and precisely.

items.prompt: Two learners measure the length of a bean root that is about 42 mm long (our own situation). One uses a ruler marked in millimetres and the other uses a rule marked in centimetres. Explain which learner can record the more precise measurement of this root.
items.canonical_answer: The learner with the ruler marked in millimetres can record the more precise measurement. In this case the smallest division is 1 mm, so the length can be read to the nearest millimetre, for example 42 mm. The rule marked in centimetres has divisions of 10 mm, so the length can only be read to about the nearest 5 mm or 10 mm, which is a much coarser value. A measurement is more precise when the scale divisions are smaller.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the ruler marked in millimetres is chosen, with the reading to the nearest millimetre, such as 42 mm (1); the reason from the data, because its divisions are smaller than the 10 mm divisions of the other rule, so it separates lengths that the centimetre rule cannot (1).
An answer that chooses the longer rule, with no reference to the scale divisions, earns no mark.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.1 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and readings are our own and unverified.
objective_titles: Decide and describe how to measure the dependent variable accurately and precisely.

items.prompt: Three replicate readings of the volume of gas collected in 60 s at one concentration are 12.0, 12.4 and 18.9 cm³ (our own invented values). Describe, in order, how the learner decides which reading is anomalous and finds the best estimate of the volume.
items.canonical_answer: First compare the three readings: 12.0 and 12.4 cm³ are close to each other, and 18.9 cm³ is far from both and does not fit, so it is the anomaly. Then repeat the 18.9 cm³ reading, or leave it out of the mean and state that it was left out. Finally calculate the mean of the readings that remain: 12.0 + 12.4 = 24.4, and 24.4 ÷ 2 = 12.2, so the best estimate is 12.2 cm³.
marking_guidance: 3 marks: the anomalous reading identified, 18.9 cm³, with the reason from the other two readings (1); the reading repeated or left out of the mean with a note, as the next step (1); the mean of the remaining readings with the working and the unit, the final result 12.2 cm³ (1).
A mean of 14.4 cm³ includes the anomaly and earns no mark for the last point. Deleting the reading without a note loses the second mark.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.1 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and readings are our own and unverified.
objective_titles: Decide whether to repeat or replicate readings, and why.

items.prompt: Explain why the mean of three replicate readings is a more accurate estimate of the true value than a single reading, when the differences between the readings are random.
items.canonical_answer: Random differences are sometimes above and sometimes below the true value, so in the mean some of them cancel each other and the mean lies closer to the true value than a single reading is likely to. A single reading carries the whole of its own difference. This holds when the differences are random, and a systematic error, which is the same in every reading, is not reduced by taking a mean.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the reason, random differences lie on both sides of the true value, so they partly cancel in the mean (1); the conclusion that the mean is closer to the true value than one reading, because one reading carries its whole difference, with the condition that the differences are random and not systematic (1).
An answer that says more readings are always correct earns no mark, because a systematic error is not reduced.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.1 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and readings are our own and unverified.
objective_titles: Decide whether to repeat or replicate readings, and why.

items.prompt: A learner prepares one tube of reaction mixture at each temperature and takes three readings from the same tube, instead of preparing three separate tubes (our own situation). Describe a limitation of this method compared with separate tubes.
items.canonical_answer: The three readings share the same preparation, so any error made in making up that tube, such as a wrong volume or concentration, is in all three readings. The readings may agree closely, which suggests a reliable result, although the tube may not represent the temperature. The effect is that the mean is not independent of the preparation error, and separate replicate tubes would reveal it.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the limitation named, the readings are repeats of one set-up and share its preparation error (1); the effect, the readings may agree even though the tube is wrong, so the result looks reliable and is not, because separate tubes would show the difference (1).
An answer that says three readings are too few does not address the limitation and earns no mark.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.1 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and readings are our own and unverified.
objective_titles: Decide whether to repeat or replicate readings, and why.

items.prompt: A labelled diagram, described here in words, shows four test tubes in a rack, numbered 1 to 4, each containing 9 cm³ of water, with a 1 cm³ pipette and a 1.0 per cent glucose solution beside the rack. Arrows on the diagram run from tube 1 to tube 2, from tube 2 to tube 3 and from tube 3 to tube 4, each labelled 1 cm³ (our own diagram). Describe, in order, how the diagram is followed to carry out a serial dilution, and state the concentration in each tube.
items.canonical_answer: First read the diagram: the arrows show that 1 cm³ moves from each tube into the next. Then add 1 cm³ of the 1.0 per cent solution to tube 1 and mix, which gives 1.0 ÷ 10 = 0.1 per cent. Then move 1 cm³ from tube 1 to tube 2 and mix, which gives 0.1 ÷ 10 = 0.01 per cent in tube 2, and repeat so that tube 3 holds 0.01 ÷ 10 = 0.001 per cent and tube 4 holds 0.001 ÷ 10 = 0.0001 per cent. Finally remove 1 cm³ from tube 4 so that every tube holds 9 cm³.
marking_guidance: 3 marks: the diagram read and the steps followed in the order of the arrows, with 1 cm³ moved from tube to tube and mixing at each step (1); the concentrations 0.1, 0.01, 0.001 and 0.0001 per cent, each a tenth of the one before (1); the final step, 1 cm³ removed from the last tube so that the volumes are equal, as the end of the sequence (1).
A series made by adding 1 cm³ of the stock to each tube does not give these concentrations, and the concentrations earn no mark.

items.prompt: State why a serial dilution must be made in the order of the tubes, with the contents mixed at each step.
items.canonical_answer: Each solution is made from the one before it, so a tube made out of order, or one that is not mixed, has the wrong concentration, and the error is carried into every later tube.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the reason, each tube is made from the previous one, so an error or an unmixed tube is carried forward, because every later concentration depends on it.
A statement that it is the method given earns no mark without the reason.

items.prompt: A learner plans to heat tubes containing a sugar solution and Benedict's reagent in a water bath at 80 °C for 3 minutes (our own situation). Describe, in order, the steps of assessing the risk of this procedure as low, medium or high, and state the level.
items.canonical_answer: First name the hazards: hot water and hot tubes can scald, and Benedict's reagent can irritate the eyes. Then judge how likely harm is and how serious it would be: harm is possible, since the water is hot, and would be moderate, since the volumes are small and the water is not boiling. The result is a medium risk, lowered by wearing eye protection, moving the tubes with tongs and keeping the bath away from the edge of the bench.
marking_guidance: 3 marks: the hazards named, the hot water and the reagent, as the first step (1); the likelihood and severity judged from the procedure, harm possible and moderate (1); the level stated as medium, with a precaution that answers a named hazard (1).

A rating of high is not supported by the procedure, because the volumes are small and there is no flame, so the result of the assessment is medium. A rating of low with no reason earns no mark for the level.

items.prompt: State why the risk of using a 1 per cent sucrose solution at room temperature is assessed as low.
items.canonical_answer: The solution is not corrosive, toxic or hot, so harm is unlikely, and a spill would have a minor effect and is wiped up.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the reason, harm is unlikely and would be minor, because the solution is not corrosive, toxic or hot.
A rating given without a reason earns no mark.

items.prompt: A leaf outline is drawn on paper ruled in 1 cm squares, so each square has an area of 1 cm². Of the squares under the outline, 31 are completely covered, 14 are half or more covered and 9 are less than half covered (our own invented counts). Describe, in order, how the area of the leaf is estimated from the grid.
items.canonical_answer: First count the squares that are completely covered, 31, and the squares that are half or more covered, 14, because both are counted as whole squares. Then ignore the 9 squares that are less than half covered. The total is 31 + 14 = 45 squares. Finally multiply by the area of one square: 45 × 1 = 45, so the area is 45 cm².
marking_guidance: 3 marks: squares half or more covered counted as whole squares, with the completely covered ones, as the first step (1); the squares less than half covered ignored, giving 45 squares (1); the count multiplied by 1 cm², with the final result 45 cm² and its unit (1).
An answer that counts the 9 squares less than half covered gives 54 cm² and earns no mark for the count. An answer of 45 with no unit loses the last mark.

items.prompt: State why a measuring cylinder is read with the eye level with the bottom of the meniscus.
items.canonical_answer: Looking from above or below makes the liquid surface seem to be at a different mark, which gives a reading that is too high or too low. Reading at eye level gives the correct value.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the reason, looking from above or below causes an error in the reading, so the reading is inaccurate, because the surface appears at a different mark.
A statement that it is the correct method earns no mark without the reason.

items.prompt: A learner tests 2 cm³ of a sugar solution with Benedict's reagent in a hot water bath for 3 minutes (our own situation). Describe, in order, how the qualitative observations are recorded in clear terms.
items.canonical_answer: First record the colour of the mixture before heating, which is blue. Then, after 3 minutes in the bath, record the colour of the liquid and of any solid with a named colour and an amount, for example orange precipitate with a yellow liquid above. The result is a record that another person can picture and compare, such as blue to orange, with the time stated, and not changed colour.
marking_guidance: 3 marks: the colour before heating recorded, the first step (1); the colour after the stated time recorded with the form of any solid, such as precipitate, in named colours (1); the record written so that it compares the before and after colours, as the final result, and not a vague phrase (1).
Words such as positive or went darker earn no mark, because they do not name the colours.

items.prompt: State why the record it went darker is a poor record of a colour change.
items.canonical_answer: It does not name the colour before or after the change, so a reader cannot picture what happened or compare it with another result.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the reason, the colours are not named, so the reader cannot tell what the change was, because darker could describe many colour changes.
A statement that it is too short earns no mark.

items.prompt:
A student plans to find how pH affects the time that an amylase solution takes to break down starch. She has starch solution, amylase solution, buffer solutions at every 0.5 of a pH unit from pH 4.0 to pH 9.0, iodine solution, a spotting tile, dropping pipettes, test tubes, syringes, a water bath at 35 °C, a thermometer and a stopwatch. She first runs a trial with three tubes at each pH. These are our own invented readings, not taken from any published source.

| pH of the mixture | Time for starch to disappear, replicate 1 / s | Time for starch to disappear, replicate 2 / s | Time for starch to disappear, replicate 3 / s |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | 480 | 500 | 490 |
| 5 | 270 | 300 | 280 |
| 6 | 150 | 170 | 480 |
| 7 | 90 | 100 | 90 |
| 8 | 180 | 190 | 190 |
| 9 | 420 | 450 | 430 |

(a) State the independent variable and the dependent variable for the main investigation, and describe how the dependent variable is measured. [3]
(b) Describe how the pH of each mixture is set, and state the range and the number of values of pH to be used. [2]
(c) Using the table, state where extra values of pH should be taken, and why. [1]
(d) Describe a suitable control. [1]
(e) State one variable that must be standardised, and how it is standardised. [1]
(f) Identify the anomalous result in the table and calculate the mean time at pH 6, showing your working and giving the unit. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) The independent variable is the pH of the mixture. The dependent variable is the time in s for the starch to disappear. It is measured by taking a drop of the mixture at regular intervals, such as every 10 s, and mixing it with a drop of iodine solution on a spotting tile, and reading the stopwatch at the first drop that stays yellow-brown with no blue-black colour.
(b) The pH is set with a buffer solution of known pH, the same volume of each buffer being added to each tube, so that the pH does not drift during the reaction. The range is pH 4 to pH 9, with at least five values at equal intervals, for example every 1 pH unit, which gives 6 values.
(c) Extra values should be taken between pH 6 and pH 8, for example at pH 6.5 and 7.5, because the shortest time is at pH 7 and the fastest rate lies close to it, so the position of the peak can be found more closely.
(d) A control tube in which the amylase solution is replaced by the same volume of water (or by the same volume of boiled amylase solution), with the same buffer, held in the same water bath for the same time and tested with iodine in the same way. The starch should remain.
(e) The temperature, standardised by holding all the tubes in the water bath at 35 °C and checking the thermometer at the start and the end. (The volumes of starch, amylase and buffer, standardised with syringes, are also accepted.)
(f) The anomalous result is 480 s at pH 6, because it is far from the other two readings, 150 s and 170 s, and does not fit the pattern of the neighbouring pH values. It is left out of the mean. 150 + 170 = 320, and 320 ÷ 2 = 160, so the mean time at pH 6 is 160 s.
marking_guidance: Table and headings: the table is given with the quantity and unit in each column heading and the body holding values alone, so the readings are read against the headings. Part (a), 3 marks: the independent variable, pH (1); the dependent variable, time for the starch to disappear, in s (1); the measurement described, a drop sampled at regular intervals into iodine and the time read when the colour stays yellow-brown, with the stopwatch (1).

Part (b), 2 marks: the pH set with a buffer of known pH, the same volume in each tube, because acid or alkali added to the mixture would let the pH drift (1); a range with at least 5 values at equal intervals, such as pH 4 to 9 (1). Part (c), 1 mark: extra values around pH 7, between pH 6 and 8, with the reason from the table that the shortest time lies there; a graph of the means with pH on the x-axis would show a minimum near pH 7, and the scale would need finer steps there.

Part (d), 1 mark: the control with the amylase solution replaced by the same volume of water or boiled enzyme, treated in the same way as the main tubes; a control left at room temperature is a different variable and earns no mark. Part (e), 1 mark: one variable with a method that fits it, such as temperature by a water bath at 35 °C checked with the thermometer; keep it the same, with no method, earns no mark.

Part (f), 2 marks: the anomalous result, 480 s at pH 6, identified with the reason from the other readings, and left out (1); the working 150 + 170 = 320 and 320 ÷ 2 = 160, with the answer 160 s and its unit (1). A mean of 267 s includes the anomaly and earns no mark. The limitation of the method, and an improvement such as sampling more often near the end-point, are not asked for here.

items.prompt:
A learner estimates the glucose in a sample of homemade fruit drink with Benedict's reagent. She makes standard solutions by a serial dilution that halves the concentration at each step. Tube 1 holds 10 cm³ of 8.0 per cent glucose solution. Tubes 2 to 5 each hold 5 cm³ of water. She moves 5 cm³ from tube 1 into tube 2 and mixes, moves 5 cm³ from tube 2 into tube 3 and mixes, and continues to tube 5, then removes 5 cm³ from tube 5. She adds 2 cm³ of each solution, of water and of the fruit drink to separate tubes, adds 2 cm³ of Benedict's reagent to each, and heats all the tubes together in a water bath at 80 °C for 3 minutes. These are our own invented observations, not taken from any published source.

| Solution tested | Glucose concentration / per cent | Colour of the mixture before heating | Observation after 3 minutes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Water | 0 | blue | blue solution, no precipitate |
| Tube 5 | to be calculated | blue | green solution, no precipitate |
| Tube 4 | 1.0 | blue | yellow solution with a little yellow precipitate |
| Tube 3 | 2.0 | blue | orange precipitate, yellow-orange liquid above |
| Tube 2 | 4.0 | blue | brick-red precipitate, pale liquid above |
| Tube 1 | 8.0 | blue | dense brick-red precipitate, almost clear liquid above |

Her record for the fruit drink reads: it went reddish and was positive. The tube was blue before heating, and after 3 minutes it held an orange-red precipitate at the bottom with an orange liquid above it.

(a) Describe how the record for the fruit drink should be rewritten in clear terms. [2]
(b) Calculate the concentration of glucose in tube 5, showing each step. [2]
(c) State the range in which the concentration of glucose in the fruit drink lies, using the table. [1]
(d) Assess the risk of heating the tubes in the water bath at 80 °C as low, medium or high, naming one hazard and one precaution. [3]
(e) Identify one variable that must be standardised so that the colours of the drink and the standards can be compared, and describe how it is standardised. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) The record should name the colour before and after, and the form of the solid: blue before heating, and after 3 minutes in the water bath an orange-red precipitate at the bottom with an orange liquid above it. Words such as reddish and positive are replaced by the named colours.
(b) Each move puts 5 cm³ into 5 cm³ of water, which gives 10 cm³ in total, so each solution is 5 ÷ 10 = 0.5 of the one before and the concentration is halved at each step. Tube 2: 8.0 ÷ 2 = 4.0 per cent. Tube 3: 4.0 ÷ 2 = 2.0 per cent. Tube 4: 2.0 ÷ 2 = 1.0 per cent. Tube 5: 1.0 ÷ 2 = 0.5 per cent.
(c) The orange-red precipitate of the drink lies between the orange precipitate of the 2.0 per cent standard and the brick-red precipitate of the 4.0 per cent standard, so the concentration lies between 2.0 and 4.0 per cent.
(d) The risk is medium. The hazard is the hot water and hot tubes, which can scald, and Benedict's reagent, which can irritate the eyes. Harm is possible but would be moderate, because the volumes are small and the water is not boiling. A precaution is to wear eye protection and to move the tubes with tongs, with the bath away from the edge of the bench.
(e) The time of heating, standardised by putting all the tubes into the bath together for the same 3 minutes with a stopwatch. (The volume of solution and of reagent, 2 cm³ each, measured with a syringe, or the temperature of the bath at 80 °C checked with a thermometer, are also accepted.)
marking_guidance: Table and headings: the table is given with the quantity and unit in each column heading, so the observations are read against the headings. Part (a), 2 marks: the colour before heating and after, both named, blue to orange-red (1); the form of the solid and the liquid described, a precipitate at the bottom with an orange liquid above, in place of the vague words reddish and positive (1).

Part (b), 2 marks: working that shows each step with the halving explained from 5 cm³ in a total of 10 cm³, 8.0 ÷ 2 = 4.0, 4.0 ÷ 2 = 2.0, 2.0 ÷ 2 = 1.0 (1); the final answer 0.5 per cent with the unit (1). An answer of 0.25 per cent halves one time too many. Part (c), 1 mark: the range 2.0 to 4.0 per cent, from the colours of the neighbouring standards; a graph is not needed because the standards are colour matches, so the scale of the estimate is the interval between two standards.

Part (d), 3 marks: the level, medium (1); one hazard named from the procedure or reagent (1); a precaution that answers the hazard (1). A rating of high is not supported, because the volumes are small and there is no flame, and a rating of low with no reason earns no mark for the level. A rating that is argued from the hazard is credited, and the hazard must be named, not only the level.

Part (e), 2 marks: one variable that could change the colour, such as the time of heating, the volumes or the temperature (1); a method that fits it, such as all tubes in the bath together with a stopwatch (1). Keep it the same, with no method, earns no mark. An improvement that narrows the estimate, such as a standard at 3.0 per cent made with the same method, is also creditworthy but is not asked for.
